algorithm.title: Algorithm E (Euclid's Algorithm)
algorithm.subtitle: Donald Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 1, §1.1
algorithm.description: Finds the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) of two positive integers through repeated remainder division.

mathematicalReading.title: Worked example
mathematicalReading.sourceNote: Following Algorithm E · The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 1, §1.1.

intro.standard: To apply Algorithm E, let $m={initialM}$ and $n={initialN}$. We begin at E1 and follow the successive divisions. In each pass, the quotient and remainder determine either a new pair of integers or the answer.
intro.withE0Swap: To apply Algorithm E, let $m={initialM}$ and $n={initialN}$. We include the optional step E0 before E1. Since ${initialM}<{initialN}$, this comparison will exchange the inputs before the first division, avoiding the initial division with quotient zero.
intro.withE0Noop: To apply Algorithm E, let $m={initialM}$ and $n={initialN}$. We include the optional step E0 before E1. Since ${initialM}\ge {initialN}$, its comparison will leave the inputs unchanged; the first division uses the given pair.

division.properFraction: Dividing ${m}$ by ${n}$ gives the proper fraction $\frac{{m}}{{n}}<1$. The quotient is therefore $q=0$, and we set $r\leftarrow {r}$: indeed, ${m}=0\cdot {n}+{r}$, with $0<{r}<{n}$.
division.mixedNumber: The division $\frac{{m}}{{n}}={q}\frac{{r}}{{n}}$ gives quotient $q={q}$ and remainder $r\leftarrow {r}$. Thus ${m}={q}\cdot {n}+{r}$, where $0<{r}<{n}$.
division.exact: The division is exact: $\frac{{m}}{{n}}={q}$, or ${m}={q}\cdot {n}$. We obtain quotient $q={q}$ and set the remainder $r\leftarrow 0$.

mathematicalReading.nextCheck: Next, E2 tests whether $r=0$; this test determines whether to return the present value of $n$ or proceed to E3.
mathematicalReading.e0Swap: Because ${m}<{n}$, E0 exchanges the inputs, giving $m\leftarrow {nextM}$ and $n\leftarrow {nextN}$. Exchanging the arguments leaves their common divisors unchanged. We proceed to E1 with the pair $({nextM},{nextN})$.
mathematicalReading.e0Noop: Here ${m}\ge {n}$, so the condition $m<n$ is false. E0 leaves $m={m}$ and $n={n}$ unchanged, and we proceed to E1 with this pair.
mathematicalReading.reduction: At E2 the test $r=0$ is false, since $r={r}\ne 0$. E3 therefore assigns $m\leftarrow {nextM}$ and $n\leftarrow {nextN}$, then returns to E1. The new pair has the same greatest common divisor: $\gcd({m},{n})=\gcd({nextM},{nextN})$.
mathematicalReading.reductionDummy: At E2 the test $r=0$ is false, since $r={r}\ne 0$. E3 therefore assigns $m\leftarrow {nextM}$ and $n\leftarrow {nextN}$, then returns to E1. Since the quotient was zero and the remainder was ${m}$, these assignments exchange the pair: $({m},{n})$ becomes $({nextM},{nextN})$.
mathematicalReading.workedReduction: Since $r={r}\ne 0$, E2 does not terminate. E3 sets $m\leftarrow {nextM}$ and $n\leftarrow {nextN}$, preserving $\gcd({m},{n})=\gcd({nextM},{nextN})$, and we repeat E1.
mathematicalReading.workedReductionDummy: Since $r={r}\ne 0$, E2 does not terminate. E3 sets $m\leftarrow {nextM}$ and $n\leftarrow {nextN}$, exchanging the inputs before returning to E1.
mathematicalReading.e0Aside: This suggests optional E0: if $m<n$, exchange $m\leftrightarrow n$. The exchange preserves the greatest common divisor and skips precisely this initial division with quotient zero.
mathematicalReading.termination: At E2 the remainder is zero, so the algorithm terminates with $n={n}$. Hence $\gcd({initialM},{initialN})={n}$. Both original integers are multiples of this answer: ${initialM}={factorM}\cdot {n}$ and ${initialN}={factorN}\cdot {n}$.

principles.title: Why the calculation works
principles.invariant: If $d$ divides both $m$ and $n$, then it divides $r=m-qn$. Conversely, if $d$ divides both $n$ and $r$, then it divides $m=qn+r$. The two pairs therefore have exactly the same common divisors, and $\gcd(m,n)=\gcd(n,r)$.
principles.termination: Every remainder satisfies $0\le r<n$. If $r>0$, E3 makes it the next value of $n$, so the positive values of $n$ strictly decrease. They cannot decrease indefinitely; eventually $r=0$. At that point $\gcd(m,n)=\gcd(n,0)=n$, and the preserved common divisors identify the answer for the original inputs.

steps_definition.name: Ensure m ≥ n
steps_definition.description: If m < n, exchange m ↔ n directly in memory.

steps_definition.name: Find remainder
steps_definition.description: Divide m by n and let r be the remainder (0 ≤ r < n).

steps_definition.name: Is it zero?
steps_definition.description: If r = 0, the algorithm terminates; n is the answer.

steps_definition.name: Reduce
steps_definition.description: Set m ← n, n ← r, and go back to step E1.

knuth_prose.opening: This explanation follows Knuth's Algorithm E. Track the pair of integers and its remainder through each phase to see how the computation reaches their greatest common divisor.
knuth_prose.start_example: For the worked example, begin with m = 119 and n = 544. Standard Algorithm E starts at E1; the optional E0 variant compares the inputs first.
knuth_prose.e1_dummy: When m < n, E1 gives q = 0 and r = m: m = 0 × n + m. E2 will test this unchanged remainder before execution continues.
knuth_prose.e2_noop: At E2, a nonzero remainder sends execution to E3. The current divisor is not yet the greatest common divisor, so another reduction is needed.
knuth_prose.e3_swap: With q = 0, the remainder equals the original m. The E3 assignments m ← n and n ← r therefore exchange the inputs. The next E1 divides the larger integer by the smaller one.
knuth_prose.e0_proposal: Optional E0 compares the inputs before division. When m < n, exchange m and n. This preserves gcd(m, n) while avoiding the initial division with quotient zero.
knuth_prose.e2_terminate: At E2, r = 0 means that n divides m exactly. Return n: the preceding reductions preserved the common divisors, so this value is also the greatest common divisor of the original inputs.

pedagogical_notes.dummy_pass_explanation: Because m < n (119 < 544), stick 544 fits 0 times into rod 119. The remainder is the entire original 119. Step E3 then sets m to 544 and n to 119. This entire division pass was wasted solely on swapping the inputs.
pedagogical_notes.e0_benefit: Step E0 inspects both integers upfront. If m < n, it executes a simple variable swap, avoiding the expensive division operation completely and reducing total passes by 1.
pedagogical_notes.geometric_intuition: Euclid's algorithm measures rod m using stick n. What remains (r) becomes the new ruler to measure the previous stick n. When a ruler fits with 0 leftover, it divides both numbers perfectly and is their Greatest Common Divisor.
pedagogical_notes.invariant_explanation: Euclidean Invariant Lemma: gcd(m, n) = gcd(n, r). Any common divisor of m and n must divide the linear combination m - q·n = r. Therefore, the GCD is conserved at every single step.
pedagogical_notes.verification_explanation: Final Verification: The resulting GCD evenly divides both initial inputs without remainder.
